contentHtml:
India’s metabolic crisis no longer needs an introduction. The ICMR–INDIAB study estimated over 100 million Indians living with diabetes and roughly 136 million more with prediabetes, with hypertension, fatty liver and obesity rising alongside. Yet the nutrition advice most people receive has barely changed in decades: eat less, cut the rice, avoid sugar, walk more. It is advice built for an average person who does not exist.

Look at the diets the world calls “balanced” and the problem becomes obvious. Carbohydrates make up about 5% of calories on a ketogenic diet and about 75% on the Ornish diet. Fat ranges from about 7% to 75%. Fibre swings nearly eight-fold. Every one of these programmes claims to be healthy, and every one contradicts the others. If “balanced” can mean almost anything, it means very little for any one individual.

Advt

Chronic Disease: Biology, Behaviour and Metabolic DysfunctionChronic metabolic diseases emerge from the interaction between biology and behaviour. Genetics, hormones, insulin sensitivity, cellular energy regulation and the gut microbiome interact with nutrition, physical activity, sleep, stress and medication exposure. Together, these influences shape how the body uses, stores and responds to energy. Every individual’s metabolic response is distinct, and that response changes with age, health status and daily circumstances. No single diet or fixed lifestyle protocol can therefore be optimal for everyone.

Pharmacological therapies remain essential: beyond improving glucose, blood pressure and lipid measurements, many treatments reduce cardiovascular and kidney complications. Yet normalising these clinical markers does not always mean that the metabolic dysfunction driving the condition has been resolved. Lasting care must also address modifiable contributors such as insulin resistance, excess ectopic fat, poor sleep, physical inactivity and nutritional imbalance — and that requires nutrition that is genuinely precise.

The Precision Nutrition IllusionIn response, a wave of offerings has emerged, marketed as “precision” or “personalised” nutrition. Most follow a familiar pattern: an app logs meals and counts calories, a questionnaire captures likes and dislikes, and a health coach, dietitian or nutritionist prepares a meal plan, adjusted for taste, region, budget and the latest lab report. Dietitians and nutritionists bring real clinical expertise, and these approaches build awareness and habit. But without continuous metabolic data, even the most expert plan is built on a snapshot. It personalises to preference and periodic tests, not to the body’s real-time physiology.

Advt

A meal plan written at a consultation, however carefully, is a static document until the next review. Metabolism is not static. The same bowl of rice and dal can be handled well on Monday and poorly on Tuesday, because between the two days the person slept badly, sat through a stressful meeting, skipped a walk or started a new medicine. Research shows that even a single night of partial sleep restriction can lower whole-body insulin sensitivity and raise post-meal glucose. A plan that sees only the plate cannot see any of this.Real precision does not begin with the plate. It begins with the person — measured continuously, modelled dynamically, and corrected at the root cause.

Advt

Real precision nutrition answers six questions together, and keeps answering them every day: what should this person eat, when, in what quantity, in what order, under what physiological conditions, and to achieve what metabolic outcome? Answering only the first — “what should I eat?” — is a diet. Answering all six continuously is precision.Restoring Metabolic Health Through Predictive Precision IntelligenceThis is where Twin Health’s Whole Body Digital Twin comes in. It is a continuously learning computational model of an individual’s metabolism, combining wearable signals, laboratory biomarkers, medication history and food logs. By integrating these inputs, its predictive models estimate individual responses to meals and personalise nutrition, activity and sleep guidance, while providing medication recommendations for the treating physician to assess. The objective goes beyond tracking glucose: it is to improve insulin sensitivity, metabolic flexibility and the physiological conditions that support healthier cellular energy metabolism.

Crucially, the lever the Digital Twin optimises is insulin demand, not calorie balance alone. A calorie is not simply a calorie: 100 calories of broccoli and 100 calories of white rice do very different things to insulin and satiety. The Twin translates its per-meal predictions into a simple traffic light — Green, Orange and Red — that a member can act on at every meal. When a meal tips into Orange, it suggests corrective levers: eating vegetables first and carbohydrates last, a smarter swap, a smaller portion or a short walk after eating.The colours are not fixed. They begin from population data and become personal, often within the first month, as the Twin learns. As metabolism heals, foods that were Red move to Orange and then Green. That shift is itself a clinical signal: the body is regaining metabolic flexibility, the ability to use glucose efficiently when it is available and burn fat when it is not.Three Layers of Nutrition, Not One NumberPopular diets argue over a single number, the macronutrient ratio, and apply it to everyone. A Digital Twin–enabled approach personalises three layers at once:

  • Macronutrients — set by predicted insulin demand, with protein and resistance targets tied to lean mass and muscle-loss risk, because skeletal muscle is the body’s largest insulin-sensitive glucose sink.
  • Micronutrients — corrected to measured gaps with attention to bioavailability, because intake is not absorption. Magnesium is the classic example: serum levels reflect only about 1% of body stores, so a “normal” report can hide cellular depletion.
  • Biota nutrients — per-person fibre, prebiotic and probiotic targets that feed a healthy gut microbiome, which in turn influences inflammation, appetite and insulin sensitivity. India’s kitchens already know fermented foods; precision decides who benefits, how much and when.

Timing and preparation matter alongside ingredients. Meal sequencing, appropriate portions and post-meal activity can help moderate glucose responses and insulin demand. Traditional practices such as soaking, sprouting and fermenting pulses or grains may improve the availability of certain nutrients, and pairing plant-based iron sources with vitamin C supports iron absorption. These strategies are personalised to dietary preferences, nutritional adequacy and clinical needs rather than imposed as universal rules.Not a Diet, and Not a RestrictionFor Indian families this point is critical. Twin precision nutrition does not ban carbohydrates or any food group. Rice, roti and millets are not the enemy; the wrong amount, at the wrong time, in the wrong order, for a particular metabolism at a particular moment, is. Members are shown their “Green for You” foods — what they can eat — rather than a list of what they cannot.The objective is broader metabolic recovery, not weight loss alone. Improved insulin sensitivity, healthier liver fat, blood pressure and lipid markers, and preservation of muscle can matter as much as the number on a scale. Mitochondrial energetics, oxidative stress and gut-derived metabolic signals offer a compelling biological framework for this approach — one that ongoing research continues to test. The longer-term ambition is nutritional freedom: greater metabolic flexibility and a wider range of foods enjoyed with confidence.Nutrition Cannot Work AlonePrecision nutrition is the most visible part of this model but only one pillar. It works alongside Precision Activity, Precision Sleep and Precision Medication, with the Digital Twin orchestrating all four as one system — giving the treating physician continuous decision support on when therapy can be intensified, maintained, reduced or stopped, while the physician retains full prescribing authority.The GLP-1 Moment: Powerful Medicines Need a Metabolic PartnerGLP-1 medicines such as semaglutide have changed the conversation on diabetes and obesity worldwide, and India is now at the centre of it. Since the semaglutide patent expired in India in March 2026, dozens of generic brands have launched, with the lowest-priced starting at about ₹1,290 a month. Medicines once reserved for a few are quickly becoming accessible to millions.The benefits are real. GLP-1 therapies lower glucose and body weight substantially, and several have shown cardiovascular and kidney benefits. But wider use has brought the debates with it:

  • Weight regain on stopping. In the STEP 1 extension study, people who stopped semaglutide regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost within a year. Many patients stop because of cost, side effects or supply, so this matters.
  • Muscle loss. A meaningful share of the weight lost — close to 40% in some studies — can come from lean mass, including skeletal muscle, the body’s largest glucose sink.
  • Nutrition gaps. Suppressed appetite can mean too little protein, fibre and micronutrients if eating is not guided.
  • Masked metabolism. These medicines can make a meal look better tolerated than it is, hiding the person’s true metabolic response.

Twin does not frame the choice as medicine versus lifestyle. GLP-1 therapy works best alongside precision treatment:

  • During therapy: the Digital Twin guides protein, resistance activity and micronutrient intake to protect muscle and nutrition while appetite is low.
  • Reading through the medicine: the Twin accounts for the drug’s masking effect when it learns food responses, and looks for a stable baseline before advancing nutrition phases.
  • Planning the next step: as insulin sensitivity, liver fat and muscle health improve, the treating physician gets continuous data to decide whether to continue, reduce or stop therapy — with the aim of stopping without regaining weight.

GLP-1 medicines can change the trajectory. A Digital Twin helps make sure the destination is a repaired metabolism, not lifelong dependence on a drug.The Evidence, and the EconomicsThis is not a theoretical promise. Peer-reviewed studies of Digital Twin–enabled precision treatment have reported remission of type 2 diabetes (Shamanna et al., Clinical Diabetes and Endocrinology, 2021). In a one-year randomised controlled trial among people with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, 68.2% of Digital Twin participants who had been on anti-hypertensives remained off them at one year, compared with none in standard care, with significantly greater falls in blood pressure (Shamanna et al., JACC: Advances, 2024).Most recently, a Cleveland Clinic-led randomised controlled trial published in NEJM Catalyst in August 2025 found that at 12 months, 71% of participants receiving Twin Precision Treatment achieved HbA1c below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medications other than metformin, compared with 2.4% receiving usual care. Mean HbA1c fell by 1.3 percentage points versus 0.3, and mean body weight decreased by 8.6% versus 4.6%. The intervention combined AI-guided personalised nutrition and lifestyle recommendations, connected sensors and human coaching.For employers, insurers and the health system, the opportunity is to move beyond participation metrics toward measurable clinical outcomes: sustained improvements in glycaemic control, cardiometabolic risk factors and medication burden where clinically appropriate. Fewer complications, hospitalisations and lower costs are important longer-term goals that require dedicated outcomes and economic evaluation. At India’s scale, precision care must demonstrate both clinical effectiveness and sustainable delivery economics.The Shift India Must MakeIndia has the scale of need, the diversity of diets, the digital public infrastructure and the AI talent to lead this transition rather than import it. But we must first be clear about what we are building. An app that counts calories is not precision nutrition. A meal plan, however expertly prepared by a coach, dietitian or nutritionist, is not on its own precision nutrition unless it is guided by continuous insight into that person’s metabolism. Precision nutrition is the right food, for the right person, at the right time, in the right context — guided by a continuously learning model of that person’s own metabolism.The old model asked people to eat less and follow the same diet as everyone else. The new model starts from a simpler truth: metabolism is personal, dynamic and repairable. Our nutrition should be too.This article is written by Dr Rohit Warrier, American Diabetes Association.(DISCLAIMER: The views expressed are solely of the author and ETHealthworld.com does not necessarily subscribe to it.
